strengths: The frequency-separated dual-branch formulation is well motivated for demoiréing: localized high-frequency texture corruption is processed using crops, while smooth low-frequency color distortion is processed after resizing. This is a sensible use of domain structure rather than a generic restoration pipeline.

The method produces competitive results on two relevant high-resolution benchmarks. On FHDMi it improves over ESDNet-L from 24.88 to 25.26 dB PSNR, 0.8440 to 0.8518 SSIM, and 0.1301 to 0.1253 LPIPS; on UHDM it obtains the best reported SSIM and LPIPS, though not PSNR.

The 6.065M-parameter model offers a favorable accuracy/size trade-off relative to most reported baselines. The paper also reports 4K computational cost and provides comparisons against both demoiréing-specific and recent general restoration models.

Ablations cover low-frequency resizing, dual-branch training, learnable composition, branch-level performance, hierarchical fusion, and RDDB components. The qualitative examples broadly support the reported reduction of texture and color artifacts.
The overall pipeline and two-stage training procedure are reasonably easy to follow, and evaluation includes complementary distortion, structural, and perceptual metrics.
weaknesses: The originality is limited. The proposed decomposition is essentially a fixed dilated Gaussian low-pass filter with a residual high-pass component, explicitly inspired by prior work, while SA-CA closely resembles established restoration Transformer designs combining channel attention, depth-wise spatial projection, gated feed-forward layers, and existing RDDB blocks. The learnable FCT is also a small convolution-plus-Transformer fusion module. The paper does not convincingly distinguish these elements from their closest technical antecedents.

The central claim that the decomposition meaningfully disentangles texture from color is supported mainly by one visualization and downstream results. There is no systematic frequency-domain analysis, measurement of leakage between components, evaluation across different moiré frequencies, or comparison with well-tuned alternative filters. The reported Haar baseline collapses to 13.32 dB, but its architecture and training adaptation are not described, making this surprisingly poor result difficult to interpret as a fair comparison.

Several ablation gains are extremely small and are reported without repeated runs or uncertainty: hierarchical fusion changes PSNR by only 0.03 dB and removing RDDB by 0.01 dB. The learnable FCT adds only 0.13 dB over fixed composition. These results do not establish that every claimed architectural contribution is robustly beneficial.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the claim that code is public: the manuscript displays no actual code URL. Important details are missing, including the decomposition level L, padding/boundary handling, feature dimensions, attention head counts, RDDB configuration, exact resizing procedure, augmentation, and baseline training protocols. There is also an unexplained discrepancy between the high-branch result in Table 5 (29.20 dB) and the nominal model in Table 6 (29.02 dB).

The efficiency evidence does not support the stronger deployment claims. Parameter count and FLOPs alone are insufficient for edge-device suitability, and 2.49 TFLOPs per 4K image remains substantial. No end-to-end latency, peak memory, throughput, tiling behavior, or measurements on an edge device are provided; the only timing ablation appears to concern a branch or patch rather than full-resolution inference.

The empirical scope is narrow: both datasets concern recaptured displays, with no cross-dataset evaluation, robustness analysis, user study, or testing on unseen devices and acquisition conditions. The paper itself notes dataset-induced color shifts, but does not separate correction of this bias from genuine moiré removal. Baseline provenance and whether all comparisons use identical data and training settings are also unclear.

Presentation quality needs improvement. There are numerous grammatical errors and imprecise statements, the inference description is internally confusing about full-resolution versus resized low-frequency processing, and the paper provides no meaningful limitations or failure-case analysis. Overall, the promising benchmark results make the decision close, but the incremental novelty and insufficiently controlled evidence favor a borderline rejection.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper presents a coherent and practically motivated design: an exact additive low/high-frequency decomposition, specialized branches using resize- and crop-based training, and learned feature fusion. The reported benchmark results are promising. On FHDMi, Freqformer improves over ESDNet-L from 24.88 to 25.26 dB while using 6.065M rather than 10.623M parameters. On UHDM, it obtains the best reported SSIM and LPIPS, although its PSNR is 0.20 dB below ESDNet-L.

The evaluation includes two high-resolution datasets, three complementary quality metrics, parameter and FLOP comparisons, visual examples, and several ablations. The resize-versus-crop experiment provides useful evidence for treating the low-frequency component globally.

The paper targets a meaningful practical problem and attempts to balance restoration quality with model size. Its decomposition also preserves spatial resolution and permits exact reconstruction by addition before learned processing.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited and overstated. The proposed decomposition is essentially a fixed dilated Gaussian low-pass filter with the residual defined as the high-frequency component; the learned FCT is convolutional projection followed by Transformer fusion. These are reasonable design choices, but the paper does not establish a substantial conceptual advance over established multiscale filtering, dual-branch restoration, Restormer-style channel attention, and learned fusion.

The evidence does not adequately isolate several claimed contributions. There is no direct ablation of SA-CA against standard channel attention, spatial attention, or a comparable Transformer block. Hierarchical fusion and RDDB yield only approximately 0.03 dB and 0.01 dB improvements, respectively, while the learned FCT gives about 0.13 dB over fixed addition and also increases capacity. The comparisons therefore do not convincingly demonstrate that the named modules, rather than the overall training recipe and parameter allocation, cause the gains.

The frequency-decomposition validation is particularly weak. The only alternative is a two-level Haar model that catastrophically drops to 13.32 dB, but the paper supplies no diagnostic analysis showing that this comparison uses a compatible architecture, targets, and reconstruction procedure. It omits ablations over decomposition depth L, dilation convention, kernel choice, cutoff behavior, and ordinary Gaussian/Laplacian-pyramid baselines. Consequently, the claimed superiority of the proposed frequency separation is not convincingly established.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The public-code URL in the abstract is blank, and the manuscript never specifies the crucial decomposition level L. Important architectural and training details are also missing, including feature widths, attention heads, RDDB configuration, padding/boundary handling, perceptual-loss layers, data augmentation, and precise inference resizing. The text is internally unclear about whether both branches process full-resolution inputs at test time or whether the low-frequency branch retains a fixed resized input.

The efficiency and deployment claims are insufficiently supported. Although parameters and estimated FLOPs are reported, there are no end-to-end runtime, peak-memory, tiled-inference, or edge-device measurements. The only timing ablation concerns an isolated high-frequency branch on an unspecified input size, so suitability for 4K inference and edge deployment is not demonstrated.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims. Evaluation is restricted to two paired benchmarks, without cross-dataset testing, robustness to unseen devices or display patterns, or convincing real-world examples. Baseline training protocols and computational measurements are not described sufficiently to verify fairness, and recent cited demoiréing/mobile approaches such as P-BiC and the real-time mobile method are not included in the comparison.

The qualitative evidence consists of only three thin, heavily reduced image strips. It is difficult to verify fine-detail preservation or residual moiré at this presentation scale, and there is no user study or region-level quantitative analysis to support the strong perceptual claims.

Overall, the method appears plausible and the numerical results have merit, so this is not a clear reject on soundness. However, the combination of incremental methodology, incomplete component validation, questionable Haar comparison, missing reproducibility details, and unsupported efficiency/generalization claims makes the scientific case too weak for acceptance in its present form.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent Algorithms/General contribution: an à-trous-style frequency decomposition, specialized high- and low-frequency restoration branches, and learnable feature-space recomposition form a well-motivated system for jointly addressing moiré texture and color distortion.

The empirical results are encouraging across two demanding high-resolution benchmarks. Freqformer gives the best reported FHDMi results on all three metrics and, on UHDM, improves over ESDNet-L in SSIM and LPIPS while using 6.065M versus 10.623M parameters.

The crop-versus-resize design is practically interesting. Table 3 shows a large advantage from resizing the smooth low-frequency component, and Table 4 provides useful evidence that frequency-specific training and learnable composition improve final-image performance over end-to-end and fixed-composition variants.

The evaluation includes PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, parameter counts, FLOPs, qualitative comparisons, component studies, and comparisons with both demoiréing-specific and recent general restoration models. The architecture and training procedure are generally understandable.
weaknesses: The central decomposition is essentially a fixed dilated Gaussian low-pass filter with a complementary residual, adapted from prior work. Its originality is therefore moderate, and the stronger claim that it explicitly disentangles texture from color is supported mainly by one visualization rather than dataset-level spectral or energy analysis. Natural high-frequency content and low-frequency moiré artifacts can violate this interpretation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The decomposition depth L is not specified, nor are several important architecture settings such as feature widths, attention heads, expansion ratios, padding/boundary handling, and VGG perceptual layers. The abstract claims public code availability, but the manuscript contains a blank URL.

The comparison set omits directly relevant recent RGB demoiréing approaches discussed in the related work, particularly P-BiC and the mobile demoiréing method. Training and evaluation details for the newly retrained general-restoration baselines are also insufficient to establish that these comparisons are controlled and equally optimized.

Some claims exceed the presented evidence. Edge-device suitability is asserted based on parameters and FLOPs, but no end-to-end latency, peak memory, or device measurements are reported; 2.49 TFLOPs per 4K image is not by itself evidence of edge deployability. The text also appears inconsistent about whether both branches process full-resolution inputs at test time or whether the low-frequency branch remains resized.

Several architectural contributions lack clean isolation: there is no direct ablation of SA-CA against standard channel attention or a matched Restormer-style block, while hierarchical fusion and RDDB yield only very small gains without repeated-run variance. The catastrophic Haar result is insufficiently diagnosed and is surprising for a perfectly invertible transform, making it difficult to know whether it reflects a conceptual limitation or an implementation/training mismatch. Overall, the evidence slightly favors acceptance, but these gaps keep the recommendation borderline rather than strong.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General. The paper presents a coherent demoiréing framework whose frequency decomposition, asymmetric crop/resize training, dual branches, and learnable composition are well motivated for separating texture corruption from color distortion.

The empirical results are consistently strong across TIP2018, LCDMoiré, FHDMi, and UHDM. Freqformer improves over ESDNet-L on most metrics while using 6.065M versus 10.623M parameters; on UHDM it obtains the best reported SSIM and LPIPS, though not PSNR.

The ablations cover the principal design decisions. In particular, the comparison against direct modeling and the large benefit of resize-based low-frequency training provide useful evidence for the central approach. Haar/DCT variants, fixed versus learnable composition, hierarchical fusion, RDDB, and projection choices are also examined.

The paper reports parameters, FLOPs, and 4K latency and candidly notes that Freqformer is slower than ESDNet-L despite requiring fewer FLOPs. Qualitative examples support improved removal of residual moiré and color artifacts.
weaknesses: The technical originality is moderate. The proposed decomposition is essentially a dilated Gaussian low-pass plus residual high-pass construction inspired by prior work [33]; FCT is convolution followed by transformer fusion, while SA-CA combines established channel attention, depth-wise projections, gated FFNs, and RDDBs. The contribution is therefore primarily the task-specific integration and training strategy rather than a substantially new transform or attention mechanism.

Evidence for the claimed superiority of the decomposition is not fully controlled. The Haar and DCT variants have substantially different parameter counts and band-specific architectures, so Table 3 conflates transform choice with network design. A parameter-matched comparison against Gaussian/Laplacian pyramids, learned filters, and alternative cutoff depths would better establish the claimed advantage.

The comparison omits some directly relevant recent methods discussed in the related work, most notably P-BiC [38] and DMSFN [27]. Comparisons to adapted RAW/video or general restoration architectures do not compensate for the absence of these specialized demoiréing baselines. Several claimed gains over ESDNet-L are also modest, and Freqformer remains worse in UHDM PSNR.

The manuscript does not adequately validate its broad frequency interpretation. Figure 2 and a single reconstruction-PSNR observation do not establish that texture corruption reliably lies in the residual while color distortion lies in the low-pass component across datasets, scales, devices, and content. Frequency-energy statistics, scale sensitivity, failure cases, and cross-dataset or real-device generalization would strengthen the scientific case.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the promised code link is blank, and important details such as learning rate, cosine-cycle parameters, padding/boundary handling, exact branch widths and attention heads, resize interpolation, and some architectural operators are missing or underspecified.

The claims of suitability for edge deployment are not supported by edge-device measurements, peak memory, or energy results. At 2.46 TFLOPs per 4K image and 0.58 seconds on an RTX 4090, the method is slower than ESDNet-L; full-resolution processing by the high-frequency branch may also impose substantial memory costs that are not reported.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated and presents an intuitively reasonable decomposition of demoiréing into high-frequency texture restoration and low-frequency color correction. The evaluation covers four established sRGB benchmarks and reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Freqformer obtains competitive or best reported results, including 25.26 dB on FHDMi and the best SSIM/LPIPS values in the presented UHDM comparison.

The model has a comparatively modest 6.065M parameters, and the paper reports parameters, FLOPs, and measured runtime rather than relying only on restoration accuracy. It also candidly acknowledges that its 0.58-second 4K runtime is slower than ESDNet-L despite using fewer FLOPs.

The experiments include useful investigations of low-frequency resizing, fixed versus learned composition, alternative decompositions, and several architectural components. The reported low-frequency resizing improvement is substantial and suggests that the asymmetric processing idea has practical merit.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General criteria, the originality is limited. The decomposition is an attributed, fixed dilated Gaussian smoothing/residual construction inspired by prior work [33]; SA-CA largely combines an RDDB with Restormer-style channel attention and a gated feed-forward network; and FCT is essentially feature projection followed by standard Transformer blocks. The manuscript does not clearly establish a substantial technical advance beyond assembling these known elements for demoiréing.

The central claim that the decomposition disentangles moiré texture from color distortion is weakly substantiated. Figure 2 contains only one qualitative example and no spectral analysis, leakage measurement, or evaluation across different moiré scales. Because the high component is simply the residual between the input and its smoothed version, it necessarily includes genuine image detail as well as moiré. The paper does not quantify this entanglement or compare against stronger learned/filter-bank decompositions.

The state-of-the-art comparison is incomplete. Recent directly relevant methods discussed in the related-work section, including P-BiC [38], DMSFN [27], and the mobile demoiréing method [52], are absent from the main tables. Conversely, Table 2 includes adapted RAW/video architectures whose input assumptions differ. This makes the broad state-of-the-art claim difficult to verify, particularly because several reported advantages over ESDNet-L are small—for example, 0.0036 SSIM and 0.003 LPIPS on UHDM—without repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance analysis.

Several ablations do not cleanly isolate the claimed contributions. The Haar and DCT variants have substantially different parameter counts and vaguely described band-specific modules, so Table 3 confounds the transform with architecture. The crop/resize study evaluates only the low-frequency branch and does not show the effect on the complete model. The paper also lacks full-model ablations for asymmetric training and SA-CA against a closely matched standard attention block. Hierarchical fusion yields only 0.05 dB, while learned FCT yields only 0.13 dB, making some novelty claims disproportionate to the evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a central algorithmic contribution. The decomposition depth L is never specified or ablated, and important architectural details such as channel widths, attention-head counts, RDDB configuration, padding, precise resize procedure, and training augmentations are missing. The promised code link is blank. The two-stage schedule also appears to require 150 epochs per stage, but the compute cost and model-selection protocol are not reported.

The qualitative evidence is narrow: Figure 6 shows only three selected cases, with small crops and no failure examples. There is no cross-dataset, cross-device, or genuinely unpaired real-world evaluation to establish that the low-frequency branch corrects moiré-induced color errors rather than learning dataset-specific capture/alignment color biases.

The deployment claim is overstated. Processing a 4K image requires 2.46 TFLOPs and 0.58 seconds on an RTX 4090, yet no memory measurement, mobile/edge benchmark, tiling analysis, or peak-resource result is provided. The method is slower than the larger ESDNet-L baseline, so suitability for edge devices is not demonstrated.

Overall, the paper has a plausible engineering idea and encouraging benchmark numbers, but the limited novelty, incomplete contemporary comparison, confounded ablations, and missing reproducibility details leave important concerns. These issues make the scientific case insufficiently convincing for ECCV acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, Freqformer presents a coherent demoiréing framework: an à-trous-style frequency decomposition separates spatially localized high-frequency artifacts from smooth color distortions, and the two components receive appropriately different crop- and resize-based processing.

The method is technically plausible and well motivated. The dual branches, learnable Frequency Composition Transform, hierarchical fusion, and spatial-aware channel attention form a consistent design rather than a collection of unrelated modules.

Evaluation is broad for this task, covering TIP2018, LCDMoire, FHDMi, and UHDM with PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Freqformer achieves the best reported results on nearly all metrics, with the main exception being UHDM PSNR, where it remains competitive.

The accuracy-efficiency trade-off is attractive: the model has 6.065M parameters and 2.46 TFLOPs at 4K, substantially smaller than several competing restoration systems. The paper also candidly reports that its 0.58 s inference time is slower than ESDNet-L despite lower FLOPs.

The ablations are reasonably comprehensive. They separately examine Haar/DCT alternatives, crop versus resize training, fixed versus learnable composition, hierarchical fusion, RDDB, projection design, and an alternative DAT architecture. Applying the resize comparison to ESDNet-L also suggests that this finding is not entirely architecture-specific.
Qualitative examples support the quantitative results, showing improved suppression of residual moiré and color artifacts, particularly on FHDMi and UHDM.
weaknesses: The central decomposition is essentially a fixed dilated Gaussian low-pass filter with a residual high-pass component, inspired by prior work. Its algorithmic novelty is therefore moderate, and the paper does not compare against simpler Gaussian/Laplacian-pyramid baselines with matched branch capacity and training procedures.

Several strong explanatory claims are supported mainly by selected visualizations or heuristic reasoning. In particular, the assertions that moiré texture is predominantly high-frequency, color distortion is low-frequency, and the components possess locality or scale robustness would benefit from dataset-level spectral measurements and failure-case analysis.

Some essential reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including the decomposition depth L, base feature widths, attention heads, RDDB configuration, exact resizing rules/scales, and complete stage-wise optimization settings. The promised code link is also blank in the manuscript.

The comparisons do not report variance across runs or statistical uncertainty, despite relatively small margins in places—for example, 0.28 dB over ESDNet-L on LCDMoire, 0.38 dB on FHDMi, and slightly worse UHDM PSNR. Accordingly, wording such as “significantly outperforms” is stronger than the evidence establishes.

All evaluation is in-dataset. Cross-dataset testing, tests on independently captured photographs, or analysis across display/camera combinations would better establish that the low-frequency branch learns general color correction rather than dataset-specific acquisition shifts.

The claim of suitability for edge deployment is insufficiently demonstrated: 2.46 TFLOPs at 4K is substantial, inference is slower than ESDNet-L on an RTX 4090, and no peak-memory, mobile-device, or energy measurements are provided.

The qualitative study contains only a few selected examples and no user study or systematic region-level analysis. Limitations and likely failure cases, such as natural repetitive textures being confused with moiré or very low-frequency moiré leaking into the color branch, are not discussed.
